title: Which of these five statements are always, sometimes or never true?
description: Five statements about sums and multiples are each tested with an example that fits and an example that fails, and the last one that holds every time is shown with algebra. Four are sometimes true and one is always true. The method is the same as the examples in the book on always, sometimes and never true.
teaching_notes: One idea: a statement is sometimes true when one example fits and another fails, and always true only when a factor can be taken out. Watch for students who call a statement always true because the examples they tried all fit.

source: Figure it Out (multiples and remainders, question 3)
video_script.why: A learner tests each of five statements with one example that fits and one that fails, and uses a factor to show the one that always holds.
video_script.substitution: the book's own five statements about sums and multiples
video_script.anchor: five statement cards, each with a fits box and a fails box, as in the book
video_script.payoff_line: The first, second, third and fifth statements are sometimes true. The fourth statement is always true.

final_answer.spoken: the first, second, third and fifth statements are sometimes true, and the fourth statement is always true

maths_rules: (i) 2 + 4 = 6, a multiple of 3; 2 + 6 = 8, not a multiple of 3: sometimes true
(ii) 10 is divisible by neither 18 nor 9, so it fits; 27 is not divisible by 18 but is divisible by 9, so it fails: sometimes true
(iii) 1 and 2 are not divisible by 6 and 1 + 2 = 3 is not, so it fits; 8 and 10 are not divisible by 6 but 8 + 10 = 18 is, so it fails: sometimes true
(iv) 6a + 9b = 3(2a + 3b), always a multiple of 3: always true
(v) 6a + 3b = 3(2a + b); 6 + 3 = 9 is a multiple of 9, 6 + 6 = 12 is not: sometimes true
video_script.design: One idea: one example that fits and one that fails make a statement sometimes true, and a factor that can be taken out makes it always true. Assumes the examples on always, sometimes and never true. The five statement cards stay on the board.

beats.on_screen: title card Always, Sometimes or Never; five statement cards in a column, each with a question mark

marks.scene: the title card arrives and the five cards appear
marks.ask: an always, a sometimes and a never box appear beside the cards

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about five statements on multiples.
<bookmark mark='same'/>We will solve it the same way as the examples in your book.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is each statement always true, sometimes true, or never true?

beats.on_screen: the five statement cards stay on the board while the child thinks

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: always: fits every time. never: fails every time. sometimes: fits for some and fails for others

marks.always: the always and never boxes light up with their meaning
marks.some: the sometimes box lights up with one tick and one cross

narration: <bookmark mark='always'/>A statement is always true if it fits every number. It is never true if it fails for every number.
<bookmark mark='some'/>If it fits for some numbers and fails for others, it is sometimes true.

beats.on_screen: Given: five statements about sums and multiples

marks.given: the five statements are written one under the other

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, there are five statements about sums and multiples.

beats.on_screen: To find: always, sometimes or never true, for each statement
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find if each one is always, sometimes or never true.

beats.on_screen: (i) 2 + 4 = 6, a multiple of 3. 2 + 6 = 8, not a multiple of 3: sometimes true

marks.fits: two plus four shows six with a tick
marks.fails: two plus six shows eight with a cross

narration: <bookmark mark='fits'/>Step one, the sum of two even numbers is a multiple of three. Two plus four is six, which fits.
<bookmark mark='fails'/>Two plus six is eight, which is not a multiple of three. This statement is sometimes true.

beats.on_screen: (ii) 10: divisible by neither 18 nor 9, fits. 27: not divisible by 18, divisible by 9, fails: sometimes true

marks.fits: ten shows a tick for the statement
marks.fails: twenty seven shows a cross for the statement

narration: <bookmark mark='fits'/>Step two, if a number is not divisible by eighteen, it is not divisible by nine. Ten is divisible by neither, so it fits.
<bookmark mark='fails'/>But twenty seven is not divisible by eighteen, and it is divisible by nine. This statement is sometimes true.

beats.on_screen: (iii) 1 + 2 = 3, not divisible by 6, fits. 8 + 10 = 18, divisible by 6, fails: sometimes true

marks.fits: one plus two shows three with a tick
marks.fails: eight plus ten shows eighteen with a cross

narration: <bookmark mark='fits'/>Step three, if two numbers are not divisible by six, their sum is not either. One and two give three, which fits.
<bookmark mark='fails'/>But eight and ten are not divisible by six, and their sum is eighteen, which is. This statement is sometimes true.

beats.on_screen: (iv) 6a + 9b = 3(2a + 3b): always a multiple of 3: always true

marks.state: the statement about a multiple of six and a multiple of nine is written
marks.write: six eigh plus nine b becomes three times a bracket
marks.always: the factor three is lit and the statement is marked always

narration: <bookmark mark='state'/>Step four, a multiple of six plus a multiple of nine is a multiple of three.
<bookmark mark='write'/>Six eigh plus nine b is three times the bracket two eigh plus three b.
<bookmark mark='always'/>The factor three is always there. This statement is always true.

marks.state: the statement about a multiple of six and a multiple of three is written
marks.write: six eigh plus three b becomes three times a bracket, showing only the factor three
marks.tests: six plus three shows nine with a tick, and six plus six shows twelve with a cross

narration: <bookmark mark='state'/>Step five, a multiple of six plus a multiple of three is a multiple of nine.
<bookmark mark='write'/>Six eigh plus three b is three times the bracket two eigh plus b. Only the factor three is certain.
<bookmark mark='tests'/>Six plus three is nine, which fits. Six plus six is twelve, which fails. This statement is sometimes true.

marks.first: twelve plus eighteen shows thirty, three times ten
marks.second: six plus nine shows fifteen, three times five

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step six, put new numbers into the always statement. Twelve plus eighteen is thirty, which is three times ten.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Six plus nine is fifteen, which is three times five. Both are multiples of three.

beats.on_screen: Answer: (i) sometimes (ii) sometimes (iii) sometimes (iv) always (v) sometimes

marks.ans: the answer line is boxed and the five cards slide into the boxes

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The first, second, third and fifth statements are sometimes true. The fourth statement is always true.
